Moving on to charts, tables and SmartArt. Numbers are much easier to understand as a chart.
Column charts compare separate things, like pupils in each house. Line charts show change over time, like visitors each month. Pie charts show parts of a whole.
Tables are good for comparing things across several headings, like the prices and features of three phones.

Now, the fun bit that people overdo. Transitions and animations.
A transition plays between slides, like Fade or Morph. An animation acts on one object on a slide.
Animations come in four types. Entrance, with a green star. Emphasis, yellow. Exit, red. And motion paths, which move things along a line.
Each one can start On Click, With Previous, which means at the same time as the one before, or After Previous, which means once the one before has finished.
And the Animation Pane lets you see them all in order and drag them around.
The golden rule is every effect needs a reason. Bullet points appearing one at a time? Great. Every word spinning in with a whoosh? Please, no.
Now links. A hyperlink is clickable text or an object that jumps to another slide, a website or a file. Control and K is the shortcut.
Action buttons are ready-made shapes, like Home, Back and Next. They're at the bottom of Insert, Shapes.
Put these together and you can build a non-linear quiz. The right answer links to a Correct slide. The wrong answers link to a Try again slide.
And here's a trap. If your Try again slide is slide seven, a Previous Slide button goes to slide six, not back to your question. So link to the exact slide.
Kiosk mode is in Slide Show, Set Up Slide Show, browsed at a kiosk. Clicks don't move the slides on, only your buttons do, and the show loops until someone presses escape.

Next, accessibility. That means designing so everyone can use your work, including people with a disability.
Alt text is a short description of an image. A screen reader reads it aloud, so someone who can't see the picture still knows what it shows.
Not image one dot jpeg. Something like, the Watergate of Enniskillen Castle beside the River Erne.
About one in twelve men and one in two hundred women are colour blind, most often red and green. So never use colour on its own to show meaning. Add a tick or a cross.
There's an international standard for all this called WCAG. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.
Its four principles spell POUR. Perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
And for contrast, WCAG level double A asks for at least four and a half to one for normal text. Black on white is twenty-one to one, the best you can get.
PowerPoint can help too. Review, then Check Accessibility, lists problems like missing alt text or slides with no title.
